**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. - artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. - loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

136:### Commit-body form
137-
138-The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
139-shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
140-problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
141-bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
142-statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
143-
144-- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
145-  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
146-  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
147-  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
148-  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
149-- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
150-  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
151-  to be more than one commit.
152-- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
153-  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
154-  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
155-- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
156-  form, the general form at its smallest.
157-- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
158-  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
159-  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.
160-
161-**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
162-pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
163-typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
164-read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
165-flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
166-a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

**Body**

```
The agent repo moved from `.claude` to `.agent-session` between
sessions, but the names pointing at it did not follow. vc-x1 resolves
the agent side from `repos.agent`, so it looked for a repo in a
directory the harness recreates empty, and every command needing both
repos stopped there.

* `repos.agent` named `.claude`, which holds no config and no jj repo.
  - It names `.agent-session`, so `validate-config` and
    `validate-agent` pass where both reported the incoherence and
    exited 1, and `vc-x1 push` reaches the agent side again. This
    commit's own push is that proof.
  - `vc-x1 symlink` now derives the link that had been made by hand,
    and reports it already correct, so config and link agree rather
    than happening to match.
* The work repo did not ignore the new directory.
  - `/.agent-session` joins `/.git` and `/.jj` in `.gitignore`.
  - `/.claude` stays beside it. The harness bind-mounts ten
    `/dev/null` nodes over `<project>/.claude` on every command and
    recreates the directory when it is deleted, a restart included,
    so the line still has work to do.
* `vc-x1 init` still hands a new workspace the old default.
  - The finding is the first `## Todo` entry rather than a fix here,
    since changing it reaches every workspace init creates and raises
    a question about the published `<name>.claude` repo names.
```
